newsitem.title: GERMANY: Concert gains momentum in global telecoms race.
newsitem.headline: Concert gains momentum in global telecoms race.

text.p: Anglo-American telecoms venture Concert is gaining momentum fast in the race for leadership in global telecommunications and could soon leave competitors behind, analysts said on Friday.

An alliance of Concert partners British Telecommunications Plc and MCI Communications Corp with Spain's Telefonica de Espana SA paints Concert's corporate colours across the map of Latin America, filling another gap in its race to achieve global reach ahead of rivals.
The deal, which includes a small equity swap between BT and Telefonica, leaves Asia as the only major economic centre not covered by Concert's sprawling communications services network.
But achieving a substantial foothold in Latin America could be the catalyst that puts Concert in the favoured position for finding a partner in Asia.

"It now appears that the Japanese have basically played a waiting game to see which of the global alliances would come out on top," Keith Mallenson, senior analyst at telecoms consultants Yankee Group Europe, told Reuters.

"This will certainly help Concert in Asia. There are still gaps but one of the most important parts of the jigsaw puzzle is Latin America and Concert's regional strengths could make it the partner of choice."
Both BT and rival Deutsche Telekom of Germany have been courting Japan's Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corp (NTT), hoping to form a partnership with the telecoms giant.
Concert is one of several alliances jostling for position as communications companies move beyond national borders to serve multinational corporate customers anywhere in the world.

The movement towards open global telecoms markets has accelerated this trend as smaller regional carriers find they must form partnerships with larger international operators or risk losing the battle for their home markets.
In a few years the lion's share of the international telecommunications market could be divided up by as few as three global carriers.
Concert's chief rival is Global One, a venture of Deutsche Telekom, France Telecom and U.S. long-distance carrier Sprint Corp.
"France Telecom has some activities in Latin America and so does Sprint but it does not compare with what Telefonica brings to Concert," said one analyst who asked not to be identified.

Global One suffered a legal setback in Germany this week when a local court ruled in favour of a BT suit that Global One had begun trading before obtaining regulatory approval. It is unclear what broader implications the ruling could have.

Deutsche Telekom chairman Ron Sommer dismissed the Telefonica/Concert alliance as a minor event. "BT is trying to do a lot of things to copy Deutsche Telekom," he said, adding that it would mean more of a weakening of AT&T, the U.S. phone giant.

Another alliance, Unisource NV, groups four mid-sized regional carriers that have sought to compete with larger rivals by combining their local strengths and teaming up with AT&T on the international market.
Unisource shareholders are Swiss Telecom PTT, PTT Telecom of the Netherlands, Telia of Sweden and Telefonica.
Telefonica's decision to joint Concert means it will leave Unisource, a major setback for the alliance which sparked an angry exchange over the terms of divorce.

"Unisource owns the data network in Spain, not Telefonica any more. We certainly will not give it (away) for free," said AT&T Unisource chairman Ben Verwaayen, adding that there were other companies interested in taking Telefonica's place.
"We don't exclude the entrance of a fourth partner. We will be carefully selecting the opportunities .. but we're absolutely not going to hurry," he said.

Analysts have speculated that Italian telecoms holding company Soceita Finanziaria Telefonica per Azioni Spa (STET) might fill Telefonica's seat. STET remains one of the few major European telecoms companies that is still not aligned with a grouping.

AT&T appears to be the main loser as a result of Telefonica's departure from Unisource. Not only does the move weaken Unisource but because it strengthens Concert, it puts more pressure on AT&T to save its floundering international strategy.
"They started with the best telecoms brand name in the world and the best position and in one way or another just fouled up," said Yankee Group's Mallenson.
